title: 25 BIZARRE Old West Truths the Movies NEVER Showed You
fullText: Forget the movie version of the Old West. The reality was brutal, dirty, and without heroes. Betrayals for money, towns that turned into cemeteries, outlaws killed by their own partners. Historians spent decades burying the most disturbing records from that era. Now, 25 documented facts reveal what really happened when the cameras weren't rolling. Get ready to learn the history nobody talks about. Subscribe to our channel and leave some hype on the video to help us out. Number one, Sam Bass, the train robber who got ratted out by one of his own. In 1877, Bass and his gang stopped a Union Pacific train [music] in Nebraska and made off with $60,000 in gold coins. That was enough money to buy a whole ranch back then. The problem is a hit like [music] that draws way too much attention. The Texas Rangers wanted bass at any cost and they got him. One of his own gang members, Jim Murphy, made a secret deal with the law. He gave up the plan for the next robbery in Round Rock, Texas. When Bass showed up in town, the Rangers were already waiting. The shootout didn't last long. Bass got shot in the back and died 2 days later on his own birthday. He was 27. In the Old West, trusting the wrong person could cost you your life. If you want the case files behind stories like this, I pinned the full dossier pack in the top comment. No pressure. It's just there if you want to go deeper. Number two, the barbed wire wars. Did you know a simple wire sparked one of the bloodiest conflicts in Texas? In the early 1880s, wealthy ranchers started fencing off millions of acres with barbed wire, blocking roads, water sources, and land that cowboys had been using for decades. The small ranchers didn't just sit back. They formed nighttime gangs called fence cutters and destroyed more than half the state's fences [music] in just two years. The response was brutal. Ambushes, homes burned down with families inside and bodies showing up on the roads. The conflict got so violent the governor had to send the Texas Rangers to restore order. An invention that cost pennies per yard ended up costing hundreds of lives. Number three, Jefferson. Soapy Smith started his criminal career on the streets of Denver in the 1880s with a simple trick. He sold bars of soap, promising that some had money bills wrapped inside. His partners [music] would pretend to buy and win right in front of the crowd. The scam sounds dumb, but it worked so well that Smith piled up enough cash to control gambling halls and bribe politicians in Colorado. When the Klondike Gold Rush blew up, he headed to Alaska to run the same setup on miners desperate [music] to get rich. His reign didn't last long. In July 1898, in a turf dispute in Skagway, a local vigilante landed a fatal shot on him. Smith was 38. Number four, the Pleasant Valley. War started over missing cattle and a torn down fence in 1880s Arizona. The Touberries and the Grahams were neighbors who turned into deadly enemies. What nobody expected was that a ranch fight would leave a trail of blood for nearly a decade. Men were hunted like animals, ambushed on their own land, whole families destroyed. When the dust settled, almost all the adult men in both clans were dead. The few who were left spent the rest of their lives looking over their shoulders. Historians still argue about how many really died because a lot of bodies were simply never found. Number five, Cath Williams, 1866. You're looking at the only documented woman who served in the US Army disguised as a man during the 19th century. Cath was born enslaved in Missouri and when the Civil War ended, she didn't have many options. So she did something nobody expected. She enlisted as William Cafe in the 38th Infantry Regiment, a unit of black soldiers. For 2 years, she marched hundreds of miles across New Mexico and Arizona, going through the same brutal training as any other recruit. Doctors examined her when she enlisted and didn't notice anything. It was only when she got seriously sick that a closer exam revealed the truth. The army discharged her immediately. No honors, no pension, no recognition. Number six, the El Paso Salt War. Did you know that in 1877, Americans and Mexicans killed each other over salt? Sounds like a joke, but it isn't. For generations, poor families from Texas and Mexico collected salt freely from the dry lakes near El Paso. It was tradition, livelihood, survival until a group of Anglo politicians and businessmen decided to fence it all off and charge for it. The Mexican community didn't accept that. What came next was brutal. Ambushes, executions, lynchings on both sides. The Texas Rangers were called in and some ended up dead. Washington sent federal troops for the first time since the Civil War to restore order in Texas. All of that over salt. It shows how greed can turn anything into a battlefield. Number seven, Billy the Kid was 21 when he died, and the law had already lost track of how many [music] people he'd killed. His real name was William Henry McCarti. He was orphaned from his mother at 14 and soon slipped into a life of crime. The funny thing is a lot of people in New Mexico saw him as a kind of old west Robinhood. He defended poor families against powerful ranchers during the Lincoln County War. But the reality was a whole lot messier. Billy killed without thinking twice. Some estimates put it at 21 deaths, one for each year of his life. Sheriff Pat Garrett finally got him in 1881. To this day, nobody really knows where the outlaw ends and the legend people created [music] begins. Number eight, the gunfight at the OK Corral happened on October 26th, 1881 in Tombstone, Arizona. Wyatt Herp, his brothers, and Doc Holiday faced off against the Clanton and McClory brothers in a clash that lasted only 30 seconds. Three men died right there. The story we know paints Wyatt as a lawman hero, but documents from the time tell a different story. Witnesses [music] said the Clantons were unarmed when the bullets started flying. Wyatt himself later went on trial for murder. He avoided conviction, but the doubt stuck around. Was that justice or personal revenge? The Hersps had old beef with that group. Some historians today believe it was a planned execution, not a fair duel. Number nine. In March [music] 1882, Wyatt Herp crossed a line a lot of people never come back from. After his brothers Morgan and Virgil were ambushed, one dead and the other mutilated, he ditched his marshall's badge and put together his own revenge squad. For weeks, Wyatt and his men hunted the suspects across Arizona with no warrant, no judge, no jury. They executed at least four men in confrontations that some people call justice and others call coldblooded murder. The federal government even issued an arrest warrant for him. Wyatt ran off to Colorado and was never put on trial. The question that remains, hero or outlaw? Maybe both at the same time. Number 10. Laura Bullan learned early on that life didn't go easy on anyone. the daughter of an outlaw. She grew up in [music] Texas around bandits and ended up joining the Wild Bunch, Butch Cassid's crew. But here's the detail most people don't know. She wasn't just another face. Laura was the gang's go-to [music] for forging checks and documents. While the men robbed trains, she handled the dirty money. In 1901, the law finally caught her in St. Lewis with stolen bills in her purse. She served her time and disappeared. She spent decades working as a seamstress in Memphis, living quietly until she died in 1961. The woman who helped steal thousands simply became an ordinary lady that nobody recognized on the street. If you want the case files behind stories like this, I pinned the full dossier pack in the top comment. No pressure, it's just there if you want to go deeper. Number 11. Clay Allison was the kind of guy you didn't want to run into on a bad day. And for him, [music] every day seemed like a bad day. This Texan [music] got a reputation in the Old West, not just for the shootouts he won, but for what he did afterward. They say he would cut off parts of the men he killed and show them off as trophies, a sick ritual that spread fear wherever he went. He survived duels, ambushes, and saloon brawls. It seemed like no bullet could take him down. But here's the part nobody expected. In 1887, Clay fell off his own wagon and the wheel rolled right over his neck. He died right there on the road. The gunman who terrorized the West wasn't taken down by any rival. It was a dumb accident that [music] ended the story. Number 12, Ned Christie. This guy was a blacksmith and a Cherokee politician respected in Indian territory. In 1887, a federal deputy turned up dead and someone pointed the finger at Christy. The problem, he wasn't even at the crime scene. Christy refused to turn himself into a white man's court that had already decided he was guilty. For 5 years, he held out on his property, building a fortified house with thick wooden walls. The marshals tried everything. Shootouts, sieges, ambushes. Nothing worked until in 1892 they brought in an improvised cannon and 40 lbs of dynamite. They blew the whole fortress apart. Christy died fighting. Years later, another man confessed to the original murder. Christy was innocent the whole time. Number 13, Lahi Dino. This woman would sit down at poker tables in Texas in the 1870s and walk away with her pockets full. The men thought they were going to get an easy win against an elegant lady. Big mistake. Lahi owned the cards like few pros of the time could. Doc Holiday played against her and walked away impressed. The funny thing is nobody really knows where she learned all of it. Some say her father taught her. Others talk about a mysterious gambler in New Orleans. After building up a fortune, she simply vanished from the saloon world. She got married, changed her name, and became a respected citizen in New Mexico. The same woman who cleaned out ranchers and gunmen ended up running charity groups. Number 14. Canyon Diablo popped up in 1881 in Arizona when the Atlantic and Pacific Railroad stopped there. Why? A 75 m canyon that would take 2 years to build a bridge across. In that time, workers and opportunists turned the place into a nightmare. The town had 14 saloons, gambling houses, and zero law. The first sheriff lasted only hours on the job before he was murdered. The ones who followed didn't have any better luck. The cemetery grew so fast it earned the nickname Boot Hill. When the bridge was finished in 1882, [music] the railroad moved on. Within weeks, Canyon Diablo completely emptied out. Today, only ruins are left in the desert, a reminder that quick fortune usually comes with way too high a price. Number 15. In 1890, a religious dance scared the US government so much that troops massacred nearly 300 unarmed Lakota at Wounded Knee. The ghost dance was born out of hunger and desperation on the reservations. A Pyute [music] prophet named Woka promised that dancing would bring back the vanished buffalo and the dead ancestors. Washington took it as an armed uprising. The army surrounded camps, confiscated weapons, and in a tense moment opened fire with Hotchkiss [music] machine guns. Women, children, the elderly. There was no distinction. Soldiers later received medals of honor. A peaceful prayer ended as one of the most brutal episodes of the Indian Wars, burying along with it the last dreams of resistance [music] from the plains peoples. Number 16.Wana Parker was the last Comanche chief to surrender to the US Army, but his story goes way beyond that. Born to a white woman captured in a raid and a Comanche warrior, [music] he spent his whole life between two worlds. After years of fighting against white expansion, Quana realized the war was lost and switched strategies. He started negotiating directly in Washington, traveling by train, staying in hotels, and [music] sitting at tables with politicians and businessmen. Here he appears in a tux, what white people wore to formal meetings, without giving up parts of his Comanche identity. The man who used to hunt buffalo on the plains was now playing the winner's political game to make sure his people survived. Number 17. In 1856, Richard Barter pulled off California's biggest gold robbery. His gang attacked a mule carrying $80,000 in gold bars. The plan went wrong when half the crew got arrested in the mountains. Barter buried part of the gold somewhere in the Sierra Nevada and went back to retrieve it later. He never managed to. In 1859, he died in a shootout with the law, taking the secret to the grave. Since then, hundreds of people have searched those mountains. Some never came back. The strange thing is nobody really knows how much gold was buried or if it's still there. But that doesn't stop anyone. Every year, new people show up digging holes, swearing they found clues everyone else missed. Number 18. Harvey Logan, known as Kid Curry, was considered by Pinkerton itself to be the most dangerous man in the Old West. That wasn't an exaggeration. While Butch Cassidy became a romantic legend, Curry did the Wild Bunch's dirty work. A specialist in taking out anyone who got in his way, he racked up at least nine lawmen kills. In 1904, after a train robbery in Colorado, he was cornered by a posi near Glenwood Springs. Wounded and with no way out, he made a choice that still puzzles historians today. He pointed his revolver at his own head [music] and pulled the trigger. Some say it was pride, others say it was fear of the gallows. The truth died with him in that ravine. Number 19. Alliances the history books would rather forget. For decades, runaway slaves found refuge among the seolles in Florida. But it wasn't just a hiding place. They married, raised families, and took up arms side by side. The US government spent more than $40 million, and lost around 1,500 soldiers trying to break that bond. There were three wars between [music] 1816 and 1858. Washington's generals didn't expect to face black and native warriors fighting like brothers. That coalition held out longer than any other slave revolt on the continent. Why did you never hear about this in school? Maybe because this story shows something a lot of people [music] would rather erase from the nation's memory. Number 20. Bill Picket wasn't just any cowboy. Born in 1870 in Texas, this son of former slaves watched how ranch dogs controlled cattle and thought, "If it works for them, it'll work for me." And it did. Pickicket would grab the steer by the horns, twist its neck, and bite the animal's lower lip until it dropped to [music] the ground. Sounds crazy, but that brutal technique turned into what we now know as bulldoging in rodeos. And the most impressive part, in a country where black people couldn't even drink from the same water fountain as white people, Pickicket became the first African-Amean star in Western entertainment, traveling the world with the famous Miller Brothers show. If you want the case files behind stories like this, I pinned the full dossier pack in the top comment. No pressure. It's just there if you want to go deeper. Number 21. After the Dalton brothers were wiped out in Coffeeville, Kansas in 1892, [music] everyone thought that story was over. But Bill Dulan, who had been a Dalton partner, decided to put together his own gang. And here's where it gets interesting. He gathered the survivors and formed what people called the Oklahoma gang. For 3 years, they terrorized banks and trains across Oklahoma territory. But the US marshals weren't going to let that slide. One by one, each member got taken out in ambushes or shootouts. Dulan himself took a shotgun blast in 1896. In the end, nobody got away. It was like the Dalton's fate had simply been passed on to them. Number 22. Curly Bill Brochious led a gang that stole cattle along the border with Mexico. In March 1882, Wyatt Herp swore he killed him in a shootout near Iron Springs, Arizona. The problem, nobody ever found the body. Some witnesses said they saw Curly Bill alive years later in Texas. Others swore Wyatt made the whole story up just to look like a hero. The truth is back then the line between lawman and outlaw was pretty thin. Wyatt had deputies who stole too. And Curly Bill, he had friends in local government. So who was the real bandit in this story? To this day, nobody knows if the man died that day or just disappeared. Number 23. In 1864, a man named Adams swore he'd found a canyon in New Mexico packed with gold. Nuggets the size of walnuts scattered on the ground like they were just ordinary rocks. He escaped an Apache attack, but he was never able to find the way back. He spent the rest of his life trying. And he wasn't the only one. Over the following decades, dozens of men headed into that merciless desert, [music] chasing the so-called mine. Many never came back. They died of thirst, exhaustion, or simply vanished. The strange part is Adams had no reason to make it up. He spent every scent he had on the search. To this day, nobody has found anything. The question is, does the gold exist or did the desert create its own legend to lure [music] in victims? Number 24. The Overland Trail wasn't for the weak. This route crossed hostile territory where stage coaches were easy targets. Passengers knew they might not make it to their destination, [music] but the promise of gold and land out west mattered more. Bandits waited at key spots and native tribes defended their land fiercely. The craziest part is that the transport companies kept operating even with the insane loss of human life. It was business, plain and simple. Anyone who climbed into those wagons was literally betting their life in a rolling game of Russian roulette. And even so, thousands made that trip. Number 25, Body, California. In 1879, this town had 10,000 people living in a crazy gold rush. Saloons ran day and night. Fights ended in gunfire, and fires wiped out whole blocks. Then the gold ran out. Within a few years, everybody left and just abandoned everything. Houses, furniture, clothes. Today, Bodie is still there, frozen in time as an official ghost town. But here's the weird part. Park rangers get packages every week. They're from tourists returning rocks, nails, anything they took from the place. The letters always say the same thing. After they took something, everything in their life went wrong. Coincidence? Maybe.

Hồi đó số tiền đó đủ để mua cả một trang trại. Vấn đề là một bản hit như [âm nhạc] thu hút quá nhiều sự chú ý. Đội Kiểm lâm Texas muốn có âm trầm bằng mọi giá và họ đã có được anh ấy. Một trong những thành viên băng đảng của anh ta, Jim Murphy, đã thực hiện một thỏa thuận bí mật với law. Anh ta từ bỏ kế hoạch cho vụ cướp tiếp theo ở Round Rock, Texas. Khi Bass xuất hiện trong thị trấn, Rangers đã đợi sẵn. Cuộc đấu súng không kéo dài lâu. Bass bị bắn vào lưng và tự tử 2 ngày sau đó sinh nhật. Anh ấy 27 tuổi. Ở phương Tây cổ, việc tin tưởng nhầm người có thể khiến bạn phải trả giá bằng mạng sống. Nếu bạn muốn có hồ sơ vụ án đằng sau những câu chuyện như thế này, tôi đã ghim toàn bộ gói hồ sơ ở phần bình luận trên cùng. Không có áp lực. Nó chỉ ở đó nếu bạn muốn đi sâu hơn. Thứ hai, cuộc chiến tranh dây thép gai. Bạn có biết một sợi dây đơn giản đã gây ra một trong những cuộc xung đột đẫm máu nhất ở Texas không? Vào đầu những năm 1880, các chủ trang trại giàu có bắt đầu rào hàng triệu mẫu Anh bằng thép gai dây điện, chặn đường, nguồn nước, đất đai mà các chàng cao bồi đã sử dụng hàng chục năm nay. Các chủ trang trại nhỏ không chỉ ngồi yên. Họ thành lập các băng nhóm hoạt động ban đêm được gọi là những kẻ cắt hàng rào và phá hủy hơn một nửa của bang. hàng rào [âm nhạc] chỉ trong hai năm. Phản ứng thật tàn bạo. Các cuộc phục kích, những ngôi nhà bị đốt cháy cùng với nhiều gia đình ở bên trong và thi thể nằm la liệt trên đường. Xung đột trở nên bạo lực đến mức thống đốc phải cử Biệt động Texas tới lập lại trật tự. Một phát minh trị giá từng xu mỗi thước cuối cùng lại cướp đi sinh mạng của hàng trăm người. Số ba, Jefferson. Soapy Smith bắt đầu sự nghiệp tội phạm của mình trên đường phố Denver vào những năm 1880 với một thủ thuật đơn giản. Anh ta bán những bánh xà phòng và hứa rằng một số bánh có gói tiền bên trong. Đối tác [âm nhạc] của anh ấy sẽ giả vờ mua và giành chiến thắng ngay trước đám đông. Trò lừa đảo nghe có vẻ ngớ ngẩn nhưng nó hoạt động hiệu quả đến mức Smith đã tích lũy đủ tiền mặt để kiểm soát các sòng bạc và hối lộ các chính trị gia ở Colorado. Khi Cơn sốt vàng Klondike nổ ra, anh ấy tới Alaska để điều hành thiết lập tương tự đối với những người thợ mỏ tuyệt vọng [âm nhạc] để làm giàu. Triều đại của ông không kéo dài lâu. Vào tháng 7 năm 1898, trong một cuộc tranh chấp sân cỏ ở Skagway, một người cảnh giác địa phương đã hạ cánh phát súng chí mạng vào anh ta. Smith đã 38 tuổi. Số bốn, Thung lũng dễ chịu. Chiến tranh bắt đầu vì gia súc bị mất tích và hàng rào bị phá bỏ vào những năm 1880 ở Arizona. Touberry và Grahams là những người hàng xóm đã trở thành kẻ thù nguy hiểm. Điều không ai ngờ tới là một trận đánh nhau ở trang trại sẽ để lại dấu vết máu trong gần một thập kỷ. Đàn ông bị săn đuổi như thú vật, bị phục kích trên chính mảnh đất của mình, cả gia đình bị tiêu diệt. Khi bụi lắng xuống, gần như tất cả đàn ông trưởng thành của cả hai gia tộc đều đã chết. Một số ít còn lại đã dành phần đời còn lại để nhìn lại của họ vai. Các nhà sử học vẫn tranh cãi về việc có bao nhiêu người thực sự chết vì rất nhiều thi thể đơn giản là không bao giờ được tìm thấy. Số năm, Cath Williams, 1866. Bạn đang nhìn vào người phụ nữ được ghi chép duy nhất từng cải trang phục vụ trong Quân đội Hoa Kỳ như một người đàn ông trong thế kỷ 19. Cath sinh ra là nô lệ ở Missouri và khi Nội chiến kết thúc, cô ấy không có nhiều lựa chọn. Vậy là cô đã làm một việc mà không ai ngờ tới. Cô nhập ngũ với tên William Cafe thuộc Trung đoàn bộ binh 38, đơn vị da đen lính. Trong 2 năm, cô đã hành quân hàng trăm dặm xuyên New Mexico và Arizona, đi thông qua quá trình huấn luyện tàn bạo giống như bất kỳ tân binh nào khác. Các bác sĩ đã khám cho cô khi cô nhập ngũ và không phát hiện điều gì. Chỉ đến khi cô bị bệnh nặng, một cuộc kiểm tra kỹ hơn mới tiết lộ sự thật. Quân đội giải ngũ cô ngay lập tức. Không có danh hiệu, không có lương hưu, không được công nhận. Thứ sáu, Cuộc chiến muối El Paso. Bạn có biết rằng vào năm 1877, người Mỹ và người Mexico đã giết nhau vì muối? Nghe có vẻ như một trò đùa, nhưng không phải vậy. Qua nhiều thế hệ, các gia đình nghèo ở Texas và Mexico đã thu thập muối miễn phí từ vùng khô hạn hồ gần El Paso. Đó là truyền thống, sinh kế, sự tồn tại cho đến khi một nhóm chính trị gia và doanh nhân người Anh quyết định để rào lại tất cả và tính phí cho nó. Cộng đồng Mexico không chấp nhận điều đó. Những gì xảy ra tiếp theo thật tàn bạo. Phục kích, hành quyết, hành quyết cả hai bên. Đội Kiểm lâm Texas được gọi đến và một số người đã chết. Washington gửi quân đội liên bang lần đầu tiên kể từ Nội chiến để khôi phục trật tự ở Texas. Tất cả điều đó đều qua muối. Nó cho thấy lòng tham có thể biến mọi thứ thành chiến trường như thế nào. Thứ bảy, Billy the Kid chết năm 21 tuổi và luật pháp có đã không biết hắn đã giết bao nhiêu [âm nhạc] người. Tên thật của anh ấy là William Henry McCarti.
